idiom_name: port interface + adapter class in its own package + record boundary models (MapStruct/Jackson for the mapping half)
implementation_notes: The classic layer is hand-written Java: the domain owns the port interface (OrderPort), the adapter sits in a separate package that is the only one importing the vendor SDK, boundary models are records (Java 16+) whose compact constructors validate invariants, and the mapping half can be generated - MapStruct @Mapper for value-to-value mapping, Jackson converters for the wire - while error translation stays explicit. What replaces the facade/adapter/translator class trio is the port plus a thin adapter and static factories (Order.from(LegacyOrder)); the fuller structure is justified when several adapters implement one port or the vendor protocol needs its own gateway object. JPMS exports or an architecture test is what actually keeps the dependency direction honest.
pitfalls: Checked exceptions are part of the vendor contract and cannot cross the port; catch and translate them at the seam instead of widening the port's throws clause.
Reflection-based bean mappers (BeanUtils.copyProperties-style) silently drop fields whose names drifted and ignore unit or null differences; prefer explicit or generated mappers.
A transitive vendor dependency on the domain's compile classpath defeats the boundary - enforce the direction with JPMS exports or an architecture test.
Records are shallowly immutable; a mutable collection in a record component still crosses the seam by reference.
